laws.name: American Privacy Rights Act
laws.threshold: Entities subject to FTC jurisdiction that collect or process covered data; small businesses (under $40M revenue, under 200K consumers) largely exempt
laws.summary: Bipartisan federal privacy bill introduced in 2024 that passed committee but stalled on the House floor. Would establish a national baseline with data minimization, consumer rights, private right of action, and preemption of most state privacy laws. As of October 2026, has not been reintroduced in the 119th Congress. Its fate and any successor bill remain the most-watched development in U.S. privacy law. Would preempt CCPA/CPRA if passed in its 2024 form.
laws.build: Not law. Nothing here is required today. Design ahead by collecting only the data each feature needs; data minimization is the core of every federal proposal and already law in Maryland.

laws.name: California Consumer Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: California Attorney General / California Privacy Protection Agency
laws.threshold: For-profit businesses meeting any: $25M+ annual revenue; buys/sells/receives data on 100K+ CA consumers/year; derives 50%+ revenue from selling personal data
laws.summary: California's privacy law, expanded by the CPRA (one statute; this record covers both). Covers sharing for cross-context advertising, not just sales. The CPPA's 2026 regulations add risk assessments, cybersecurity audits for larger businesses, and rules for automated decision-making technology (ADMT compliance from January 1, 2027). Limited private right of action for data breaches.
laws.build:
- "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" link in the footer (or one combined opt-out link)
- "Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information" link if you use sensitive data beyond what's needed to provide the service
- Treat Global Privacy Control (GPC) browser signals as a valid opt-out, with no extra steps
- Notice at collection shown at or before the point data is collected (sign-up forms, SDKs, apps)
- Privacy policy updated at least every 12 months, including retention periods per data category
- At least two ways to submit requests; confirm receipt within 10 business days, respond within 45 days, process opt-outs within 15 business days
- Access, deletion, correction, and portability workflows with identity verification
- No dark patterns: opting out can't take more steps than opting in
- Data minimization: collect only what is reasonably necessary for disclosed purposes
- Risk assessments before high-risk processing; ADMT notice and opt-out for significant decisions from January 1, 2027
- CCPA-compliant contracts with service providers, contractors, and third parties
- No penalty or degraded service for exercising rights (financial incentives need a notice)
laws.next: January 1, 2027: automated decision-making technology (ADMT) notice, opt-out and access rules apply.

laws.name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act
laws.threshold: Operators of websites/online services directed to children under 13, or with actual knowledge of collecting data from children under 13
laws.summary: Federal law restricting online collection of personal information from children under 13. Requires verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing a child's personal information. Operators must post clear privacy notices, allow parents to review and delete their child's data, and maintain reasonable data security. The FTC's amended COPPA Rule (first update since 2013) became enforceable April 22, 2026: it requires separate parental consent before disclosing children's data to third parties such as advertisers, a written data retention policy, and a written children's information security program. FTC enforces; no private right of action. COPPA 2.0 (teen coverage) passed the Senate in March 2026 but is not law.
laws.build:
- Neutral age screen that doesn't nudge kids to lie about their age
- Verifiable parental consent before collecting any personal information from children under 13
- Separate parental consent before disclosing children's data to third parties such as advertisers (amended rule, enforceable April 22, 2026)
- Direct notice to parents and an online privacy notice describing data practices
- Parent dashboard or process to review, delete, and revoke consent for their child's data
- Written data retention policy; delete children's data once it's no longer needed
- Written children's information security program
- Don't require more data than reasonably necessary for a child to participate

laws.name: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act 2.0
laws.threshold: As proposed: operators of websites and online services directed to children under 13 or teens under 17, or with actual knowledge (or knowledge fairly implied) of users under 17
laws.summary: NOT LAW. The Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act passed the Senate unanimously on March 5, 2026 and is stalled in the House as of mid-2026. If enacted, it would extend COPPA protections to teens 13-16 and ban targeted advertising to minors. Product teams should design for it but are not yet bound by it. The binding change this year is the FTC's amended COPPA Rule (see COPPA record), enforceable April 22, 2026.
laws.build:
Not law. Nothing here is required today. If you want to design ahead of it:
- Build age signals into your product so you can identify users under 17
- Architect ad systems so targeted ads can be switched off for minors
- Build an 'eraser button' so parents and teens can delete teen data
Several states (Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, Colorado) already restrict targeted ads and data sales for known minors, so much of this is required at the state level now.

laws.name: Colorado Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ CO consumers/year, or 25K+ CO consumers/year and deriving revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Colorado's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2023. Grants residents rights to access, correct, delete, port data, and opt out of sale, targeted advertising, and profiling. Requires data protection assessments for high-risk processing and opt-in consent for sensitive data. Universal opt-out mechanisms (like GPC) must be honored as of July 1, 2024. AG enforces; no private right of action.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice meeting Colorado's rule-specified content requirements
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals such as GPC
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data, with refresh of consent at set intervals per the Colorado rules
- No dark patterns in consent flows
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing, kept on file
- Known minors under 18 (since Oct 1, 2025): consent before targeted ads, sale, or profiling, and assess heightened risk of harm to minors
- Biometric data (since July 1, 2025): written retention and deletion policy and consent, regardless of the user-count threshold
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Connecticut Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: As amended by SB 1295 (effective July 1, 2026): controllers that process data of 35K+ CT consumers/year, OR process any sensitive data, OR offer any personal data for sale. The old 25K/25%-revenue prong is gone.
laws.summary: Connecticut's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2023. SB 1295 (effective July 1, 2026) lowered the threshold to 35K consumers and now covers anyone processing sensitive data or selling personal data regardless of volume. It added rights to contest profiling decisions and to get a list of third parties that bought the consumer's data, added neural data, financial credentials and government ID numbers to sensitive data, and requires privacy notices to disclose whether data trains LLMs. SB 4 (effective October 1, 2026) bans selling precise geolocation data; data broker registration starts January 1, 2027. Opt-in for sensitive data; universal opt-out signals honored. AG enforces; fines up to $5,000 per willful violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice stating whether personal data is used to train large language models, request methods, and month/year last updated
- Request flow for access (including inferences), correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- List of third parties that bought a consumer's data, available on request
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling; honor GPC and other universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data, which now includes neural data, financial account credentials, and government ID numbers
- Profiling decisions with legal or similar effects: explain the reason, let users review data and contest the result, and run an impact assessment
- From October 1, 2026: do not sell precise geolocation data
- Never return SSNs, account numbers, or similar identifiers in access responses
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Delaware Personal Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ DE consumers/year, or 10K+ DE consumers/year and deriving 20%+ revenue from personal data sales (lower thresholds than most states)
laws.summary: Delaware's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. Low thresholds (35K consumers). Opt-in consent for sensitive data and consent before selling or targeting ads to known teens 13-17. Consumers can get a list of specific third parties that received their data. Universal opt-out signals required from January 1, 2026. The 60-day cure period ran through 2025 and is now at the AG's discretion. Civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- List of specific third parties that received a consumer's data, available on request
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals (required from January 1, 2026)
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Consent before selling or targeting ads to consumers you know are 13-17
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: U.S. Department of Education (Student Privacy Policy Office)
laws.threshold: Educational agencies and institutions that receive federal funding from the U.S. Department of Education
laws.summary: Federal law protecting the privacy of student education records. Gives parents (and students over 18) rights to access, review, and request amendment of education records. Schools generally cannot disclose education records without written consent, with exceptions (school officials, transfer schools, financial aid, judicial orders, health/safety emergencies). Enforced by withholding federal funds; no private right of action.
laws.build:
Applies to schools; ed-tech vendors are bound through the school contract (the 'school official' exception).
- Use student records only for the purpose the school authorized
- No re-disclosure of student records to other parties without school authorization
- No advertising or profiling using student education records
- Let the school control the data: support access, amendment, and deletion requests routed through the school
- Delete or return student data at contract end
- Check state student privacy laws too (California SOPIPA and similar), which often add stricter vendor rules

laws.name: General Data Protection Regulation
laws.threshold: Any org processing EU resident personal data, regardless of where the org is located
laws.summary: Landmark EU regulation establishing comprehensive data protection rights. Requires lawful basis for processing, data minimization, and purpose limitation. Imposes strict breach notification (72 hrs), DPIAs for high-risk processing, and appointment of DPOs. Fines up to 4% global annual revenue or €20M.
laws.build:
- Document a lawful basis (consent, contract, legitimate interests, etc.) for each processing purpose before launch
- Cookie consent banner: no non-essential cookies or trackers until the user opts in (ePrivacy rules), with reject as easy as accept
- Privacy notice meeting Articles 13-14
- Request flow for access, deletion, correction, portability, restriction, and objection, answered within one month
- Records of processing activities (Article 30)
- DPIA before high-risk processing (large-scale profiling, sensitive data, systematic monitoring)
- Data processing agreements with every vendor; Standard Contractual Clauses or EU-US Data Privacy Framework certification for transfers to the US
- Breach detection and a process to notify the regulator within 72 hours
- Privacy by design and default: minimal data collection and privacy-protective settings out of the box
- EU representative if you have no EU establishment; DPO if required

laws.name: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act
laws.enforcer: FTC, federal banking regulators (OCC, FDIC, Fed, NCUA)
laws.threshold: Financial institutions that are significantly engaged in financial activities and their affiliates
laws.summary: Federal law requiring financial institutions to explain data-sharing practices and protect customer financial information. Three main rules: Financial Privacy Rule (annual privacy notices, opt-out of sharing with non-affiliates); Safeguards Rule (information security program — significantly updated in 2023); Pretexting Rule (prohibits social engineering to access financial records). No private right of action; enforced by FTC and banking regulators.
laws.build:
- Initial privacy notice at account opening, and annual notices unless you qualify for the exception
- Opt-out before sharing customer data with nonaffiliated third parties (with listed exceptions)
- Safeguards Rule: written information security program run by a named qualified individual
- Encryption of customer information in transit and at rest, and MFA for anyone accessing it
- Written risk assessment, regular testing, and vendor oversight
- Notify the FTC within 30 days of discovering a breach affecting 500 or more consumers
- No pretexting: build identity checks so callers can't social-engineer account data

laws.name: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
laws.threshold: Covered entities (health plans, providers, clearinghouses) and their business associates
laws.summary: Federal law protecting health information (PHI) held by covered entities and their business associates. Privacy Rule sets standards for PHI use and disclosure; Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI. Breach Notification Rule requires notice to individuals, HHS, and sometimes media. No private right of action — enforcement by HHS OCR with civil and criminal penalties.
laws.build:
- Signed Business Associate Agreement with every vendor that touches PHI (cloud hosting, analytics, support tools, AI vendors)
- Access controls, unique user IDs, audit logs, and encryption for electronic PHI
- Use and show only the minimum necessary PHI for each function
- Patient access requests fulfilled within 30 days, in the format requested where feasible
- Do not send PHI to advertising or analytics pixels and SDKs without a BAA
- Written risk analysis and risk management plan under the Security Rule
- Breach notification to individuals within 60 days of discovery

laws.name: Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: Private right of action (no state agency enforces)
laws.threshold: Private entities that collect, capture, purchase, receive, or otherwise obtain biometric identifiers or information from Illinois residents
laws.summary: Illinois law governing collection and use of biometric identifiers (fingerprints, retina/iris scans, voiceprints, face geometry, hand scans). Requires written policy, informed written consent before collection, and prohibits sale of biometric data. Strict private right of action: $1,000–$5,000 per violation plus attorneys' fees, regardless of actual harm. Has generated massive class action litigation. 2024 amendment addressed statute of limitations questions.
laws.build:
Applies to any face, fingerprint, voiceprint, iris, or hand scan, including features like face-based photo tagging, voice login, or ID verification.
- Public written policy with a retention schedule and destruction rules
- Written notice of what is collected, why, and for how long, then a signed written release (electronic signature counts) before collecting
- Never sell, lease, trade, or profit from biometric data
- No disclosure to vendors without consent
- Destroy biometric data when the purpose is met or within 3 years of the user's last interaction, whichever comes first
- Store and protect it at least as well as other confidential data
Private right of action: liquidated damages per person ($1,000 negligent, $5,000 reckless), so get this right before launch

laws.name: Indiana Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ IN consumers/year, or 25K+ IN consumers/year and deriving over 50% of revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Indiana's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2026. Closely modeled on Virginia's VCDPA. Opt-in consent for sensitive data; data protection assessments required. Correction right limited to data the consumer provided. AG enforces with a permanent 30-day cure period; up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and data copy, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Iowa Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ IA consumers/year, or 25K+ IA consumers/year and deriving 50%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Iowa's privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. One of the more limited state laws — no correction right, no opt-out of targeted advertising or profiling, no data protection assessment requirement, and sensitive data requires opt-out (not opt-in). 90-day cure period (longest of any state law). AG enforces; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, deletion, and portability with a 90-day response clock and appeal process
- Opt-out of sale
- Clear notice and an opt-out before processing sensitive data (Iowa does not require opt-in)
- Reasonable data security
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ KY consumers/year, or 25K+ KY consumers/year and deriving over 50% of revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Kentucky's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2026. Closely modeled on Virginia's VCDPA. Consent required for sensitive data; data protection assessments required. AG enforces with a 30-day cure period; up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Consent screen before collecting sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Maryland Online Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ MD consumers/year, or 10K+ MD consumers/year and deriving 20%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Maryland's comprehensive privacy law, effective October 1, 2025. One of the most protective state laws — prohibits processing of sensitive data unless strictly necessary (stronger than opt-in consent). Also prohibits selling sensitive data outright in most cases. Requires data minimization: controllers may only process data that is reasonably necessary and proportionate. AG enforces; civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation (first offense) and $25,000 per subsequent violation.
laws.build:
- Collect only data that is reasonably necessary and proportionate to the service the user asked for; this is a hard limit, not a disclosure
- Sensitive data: collect or process only when strictly necessary to provide the requested service; consent does not cure it
- Never sell sensitive data
- No sale or targeted advertising to users you know, or should have known, are under 18
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Data protection assessment for each algorithm used in high-risk processing
- Applies to processing activities from April 1, 2026; audit existing data flows against the necessity standard

laws.name: Minnesota Consumer Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ MN consumers/year, or 25K+ MN consumers/year and deriving 25%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Minnesota's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 31, 2025. Adds a right to a list of specific third parties that received a consumer's data, a right to question profiling decisions, and a written data inventory requirement. Controllers must give a reason when denying a request. Opt-in for sensitive data and data protection assessments. AG enforces; the 30-day cure period ended January 31, 2026. Civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock; explain the reason when denying a request
- List of specific third parties that received a consumer's data, available on request
- Right to question profiling results: tell users the reason for a significant decision and let them review data and request re-evaluation
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data; no sale or targeted ads to known users under 16 without consent
- Written data inventory and documented privacy and security policies
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Montana Consumer Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: As amended by SB 297 (effective Oct 1, 2025): controllers processing data of 25K+ MT consumers/year, or 15K+ MT consumers/year and deriving 25%+ revenue from personal data sales. Some provisions reach any business targeting Montana residents.
laws.summary: Montana's comprehensive privacy law, effective October 1, 2024, and significantly amended by SB 297 effective October 1, 2025. The amendment cut the threshold from 50K to 25K consumers, eliminated the cure period entirely, narrowed the GLBA exemption to banks and credit unions, required a labeled opt-out link, and barred disclosing SSNs and account numbers in access responses. Requires opt-in consent for sensitive data. AG enforces with no cure period; fines up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice with the content required by the 2025 amendment, including a clearly labeled opt-out link
- Notify users of material privacy changes and let them withdraw earlier consent
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Never return SSNs, account numbers, or similar identifiers in access responses
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- No cure period: the AG can act on the first violation

laws.name: Nebraska Data Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Any business processing Nebraska residents' data that is not an SBA-defined small business. No consumer-count or revenue threshold. Small businesses still need consent to sell sensitive data.
laws.summary: Nebraska's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. Follows the Texas model: coverage depends on not being an SBA small business rather than on user counts. Opt-in consent for sensitive data, data protection assessments for high-risk processing. AG enforces with a permanent 30-day cure period; up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and data copy, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data (health, precise location, biometrics, race, religion, sexual orientation, immigration status, children's data)
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: New Hampshire Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ NH consumers/year, or 10K+ NH consumers/year and deriving 25%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: New Hampshire's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2025. Closely modeled on Connecticut's CTDPA. Requires opt-in for sensitive data, data protection assessments for high-risk processing, and honoring universal opt-out signals. AG enforces with 60-day cure period through January 1, 2026, then discretionary. Civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Consent before selling or targeting ads to consumers you know are 13-15
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: New Jersey Data Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs (Attorney General)
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ NJ consumers/year (excluding payment processing), or 25K+ NJ consumers/year and deriving revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: New Jersey's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 15, 2025. Any revenue from selling personal data triggers coverage at 25K consumers, with no percentage floor. Broad sensitive data definition that includes financial information. Opt-in for sensitive data; assessments before high-risk processing starts. AG enforces; no private right of action. The 30-day cure period ended in July 2026.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals (required since July 15, 2025)
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data, which includes financial information and status as transgender or non-binary
- Consent before selling, targeting ads to, or profiling consumers you know are 13-17
- Data protection assessment before starting high-risk processing, not after
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Oregon Consumer Privacy Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 100K+ OR consumers/year (excluding payment-only data), or 25K+ OR consumers/year and deriving 25%+ of gross revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Oregon's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2024. Covers nonprofits beginning July 1, 2025 (most state laws exempt them). Consumers can get a list of the specific third parties that received their data. A 2025 amendment bans selling precise geolocation data and data of known consumers under 16, effective January 1, 2026. Requires opt-in for sensitive data and honoring universal opt-out signals. AG enforces; no private right of action. 30-day cure ended January 1, 2026.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- List of the specific third parties that received a consumer's data, available on request
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Do not sell precise geolocation data or the data of consumers you know are under 16 (2025 amendment, effective January 1, 2026)
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Nonprofits are covered: don't assume an exemption
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers processing data of 35K+ RI consumers/year (excluding payment-only data), or 10K+ RI consumers/year and deriving over 20% of revenue from personal data sales. Every commercial website collecting RI customer data must post a privacy notice regardless of size.
laws.summary: Rhode Island's comprehensive privacy law, effective January 1, 2026. Low thresholds (35K consumers). Opt-in for sensitive data; data protection assessments; privacy notice must name third parties data is sold to. A separate notice duty applies to every commercial website regardless of size. AG enforces with no cure period; up to $10,000 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories collected and every third party you sell to or may sell to (required for all commercial websites, even below the thresholds)
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
- No cure period: ship compliant, there is no warning letter

checker.dutyBelow: Every commercial website collecting Rhode Island customer data must post a privacy notice, even below the thresholds.

laws.name: Tennessee Information Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers with $25M+ annual revenue that process data of 175K+ TN consumers/year, or 25K+ TN consumers/year and deriving 50%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Tennessee's comprehensive privacy law, effective July 1, 2025. Unique feature: a safe harbor for companies that adopt and adhere to a nationally recognized privacy framework (e.g., NIST Privacy Framework). $25M revenue floor limits applicability to larger companies. 60-day cure period. AG enforces; civil penalties up to $15,000 per violation — one of the higher penalty caps among state laws.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling
- Opt-in consent for sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Optional but valuable: a written privacy program aligned to the NIST Privacy Framework gives you an affirmative defense
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Texas Data Privacy and Security Act
laws.threshold: Any entity that conducts business in Texas or produces products/services consumed by TX residents and processes personal data — no revenue or volume thresholds (broad applicability); small businesses as defined by SBA are exempt
laws.summary: Texas's comprehensive state privacy law, effective July 1, 2024. Notable for having no revenue or data volume thresholds — any business processing TX resident data that isn't a small business may be covered. Grants access, correction, deletion, portability, and opt-out rights (sale, targeted advertising, profiling). AG enforces with 30-day cure period; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation. Universal opt-out mechanism must be honored.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- If you sell sensitive data, the exact notice text: "NOTICE: We may sell your sensitive personal data." (Biometric sales need their own version)
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock and appeal process
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and profiling; honor universal opt-out signals
- Opt-in consent before processing sensitive data; even SBA small businesses must get consent before selling sensitive data
- Data protection assessment before high-risk processing
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Utah Consumer Privacy Act
laws.enforcer: Utah Attorney General / Division of Consumer Protection
laws.threshold: Controllers with $25M+ annual revenue that process data of 100K+ UT consumers/year, or 25K+ UT consumers/year and derive 50%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Utah's privacy law, effective December 31, 2023. The most business-friendly state law: requires $25M revenue plus a volume threshold, has no data protection assessment requirement, and sensitive data needs only notice and an opt-out. Permanent 30-day cure period. AG and Division of Consumer Protection enforce; civil penalties up to $7,500 per violation.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, deletion, and portability with a 45-day response clock
- Opt-out controls for sale and targeted advertising
- Clear notice and an opt-out before processing sensitive data (Utah does not require opt-in)
- Reasonable data security
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you

laws.name: Virginia Consumer Data Protection Act
laws.threshold: Controllers that process data of 100K+ VA consumers/year, or 25K+ VA consumers/year and derive 50%+ revenue from personal data sales
laws.summary: Virginia's comprehensive state privacy law, effective January 1, 2023. Grants consumers rights to access, correct, delete, port, and opt out of sale, targeted advertising, and profiling. Controllers must conduct data protection assessments for high-risk processing. No private right of action — AG enforces with 30-day cure period and up to $7,500 per violation. Exemptions for HIPAA-covered entities, FERPA-covered institutions, nonprofits, and government entities.
laws.build:
- Privacy notice listing data categories, purposes, third parties, and how to exercise rights
- Request flow for access, correction, deletion, and portability, with identity verification and a 45-day response clock
- Appeal process for denied requests, with a link to the AG complaint form
- Opt-out controls for sale, targeted advertising, and significant-decision profiling
- Opt-in consent screen before collecting sensitive data; parental consent for known children under 13
- Data protection assessment before launching targeted ads, data sales, profiling, or sensitive-data features
- Contracts with every vendor that processes personal data for you
